Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Mr. James Okonkwo is a 68-year-old African widower who works as a policy analyst in Washington D.C. Eight months ago, Mr. Okonkwo was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that required extensive hospitalization and treatment. The experience left him feeling both physically and emotionally vulnerable. Since his diagnosis, Mr. Okonkwo has found it challenging to concentrate at work. He describes difficulty focusing on tasks and feeling constantly tense and ready to react to any signs of danger. This heightened state persists even when he is inside his own home, where he feels on guard and hypervigilant. What frightens him most is that his body continues to react as if he were still in a life-threatening situation, despite being safe. The memories of his illness often feel like they are happening right now rather than something that has passed, leaving Mr. Okonkwo feeling overwhelmed by emotion each time they return. During these moments, he feels numb and detached from the experience, as if it happened to someone else. The intensity of these emotions disrupts his daily routine, forcing him to pause whatever he is doing until he can regain some semblance of composure. Mr. Okonkwo’s negative appraisals exacerbate his feelings of threat and vulnerability. He has come to believe that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again and that his body is unreliable. This belief makes it harder for him to trust himself and his environment, leading to a cycle where his constant sense of threat reinforces these negative thoughts about his own emotional capacity. For example, when Mr. Okonkwo experiences difficulty concentrating at work, he often feels overwhelmed by the memory of his illness. The vividness of those memories makes it challenging for him to focus on his job responsibilities, leading to increased tension and hypervigilance. This cycle then reinforces his negative appraisal that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger. In addition to these core symptoms, Mr. Okonkwo occasionally has moments when the memory of his illness seems distant and almost surreal. However, these fleeting instances do not provide him with much relief, as they are often overshadowed by the more potent memories that leave him feeling on edge. The constant tension and hypervigilance have affected Mr. Okonkwo’s work performance, leading to missed deadlines and a decline in his overall productivity. His colleagues have noticed changes in his demeanor and express concern about his well-being. Despite this, Mr. Okonkwo has found it difficult to open up about the underlying reasons for his struggles. What finally brought Mr. Okonkwo to seek help was an incident where he had a panic attack at work, leaving him feeling humiliated and isolated. This experience underscored for him that the symptoms were no longer manageable on his own. He is most afraid of losing control in front of his colleagues again but hopes that therapy will provide him with tools to regain some sense of normalcy and emotional stability. Mr. Okonkwo’s narrative illustrates a self-reinforcing cycle where negative appraisals about his body and emotions fuel his heightened threat response, which in turn makes the memories more vivid and overwhelming. The result is a persistent state of hypervigilance that affects nearly every aspect of his life, from work to personal well-being.
